page: Microsoft Azure FX16mds_v2 is a compute and memory intensive virtual machine running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. The instance is powered by an x86_64 Intel Xeon 8573C processor operating at 4.2 GHz, allocating 16 dedicated vCPUs across 8 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading. It features substantial cache levels, including 260 MB of L3 cache, alongside support for advanced instruction sets including AVX-512, AMX Tile, and AMX INT8. Memory capacity is configured at 336.0 GB of RAM, providing a dense ratio of 21.0 GB per vCPU. Local ephemeral storage is bundled via a 945 GB NVMe SSD, and the instance operates without discrete GPU accelerators.

Benchmark results demonstrate strong single-thread execution efficiency driven by the 4.2 GHz clock rate. The instance scored 2217.0 in Geekbench single-core testing and reached 429.6 tokens per second in small model LLM text generation, placing both results in the top tier. Data compression benchmarks also yielded strong results, achieving 34.55 GB/sec in single-threaded gzip compression and 14.35 GB/sec in single-threaded bzip3 decompression. Geekbench text processing performed in the top tier at 2988.0, and image processing registered in the top 25 percent. Conversely, broader multi-core metrics, stress-ng benchmarks, and Redis throughput (25.14 million operations/sec) clustered in the median 50 percent range, while PassMark memory testing scored in the bottom 25 percent.

The qualitative economic profile of the FX16mds_v2 reflects a specialized configuration that trades core count for very high clock speed and an unusually high memory-to-core ratio. The bundled high-speed NVMe storage lowers secondary storage requirements for temporary scratch files or working buffers. However, the presence of only 8 physical cores limits parallel scale compared to general multi-core instances of similar memory footprints.

The hardware profile suits memory-intensive enterprise applications requiring high per-core performance and large working sets. Primary workloads include in-memory databases, electronic design automation (EDA), complex financial modeling, analytics pipelines requiring fast single-thread throughput, and mid-sized cache layers benefiting from bundled NVMe scratch space.
